name: Albireo
notes: The undisputed king of colored double stars! High color contrast easily resolved even in a 50mm finder scope.

name: Algieba
notes: Spectacular pair of giant golden stars in Leo's Mane! One of the finest spring double stars in any small telescope.

name: Mizar & Alcor / Mizar AB
notes: Historic first telescopic double star (split by Riccioli in 1650). Telescopic pair Mizar A & B split easily at 40x.

name: Castor
notes: Splendid binary system with orbit period of ~445 years. Beautiful equal-brightness pair requiring 70mm+ scope.

name: Almach
notes: Often considered even more beautiful than Albireo! Striking golden-orange primary with a rich indigo-blue companion.

name: Alrescha
notes: The knot of the Pisces ribbon! Classic close binary system. Split nicely in 85mm-100mm refractors at 120x+.

name: Revati (Zeta Piscium)
notes: Pleasant wide double star in Pisces. Easily resolved in small 60mm refractors.

name: 55 Piscium
notes: Striking orange giant primary with a faint blue companion. High contrast pair for 75mm+ scopes.

name: 32 Orionis
notes: Classic Dawes' limit test target! Separation 1.3" requires steady seeing and 100mm+ scope at 150x+.

name: Propus
notes: Tight visual binary with reddish giant primary. Excellent resolution challenge for 90mm-100mm scopes.

name: Cor Caroli
notes: Named 'Charles's Heart' in honor of King Charles II. Wide separation and lovely soft color contrast.

name: Mesarthim
notes: Identical twin white stars split like headlights in the sky. Discovered by Hooke in 1664.

name: Lambda Arietis
notes: Wide yellow-white primary with sky blue companion. Very easy target for small refractors.

name: Gamma Delphini
notes: Located at the snout of the Dolphin. Golden yellow primary and pale emerald-turquoise secondary.

name: STF 2725 (Delphinus Saddle Gem)
notes: Located in the same low-power field as Gamma Delphini! Delightful secondary pair.

name: Ras Algethi
notes: Red supergiant primary with a blue-green companion. High contrast tight pair requiring 80x+ magnification.

name: Achird
notes: Nearby sun-like binary system (19 light-years). Warm yellow primary with a dim reddish-orange dwarf secondary.

name: Acrab
notes: Bright summer pair at the head of the Scorpion. Very easy to resolve in any small telescope.

name: Porrima
notes: Famous 169-year binary system. Currently widening after periastron in 2005. Requires 100x+.

name: Zubra / Spring Albireo
notes: Affectionately called the 'Spring Albireo' due to its striking yellow and sapphire blue color contrast.

name: Kurhah
notes: Neat double star in circumpolar Cepheus. Crisp contrast between primary and soft violet companion.

name: Alfirk (Beta Cephei)
notes: Bright B-type subgiant variable star accompanied by a pale sapphire companion.

name: Epsilon-1 Lyrae (Double-Double)
notes: Northern component of the famous Double-Double! Tests telescope optics. Requires 120x+.

name: Epsilon-2 Lyrae (Double-Double)
notes: Southern component of the Double-Double, oriented nearly perpendicular to Epsilon-1.

name: Rigel
notes: Classic high-contrast test! The brilliant glare of Rigel A makes locating the companion tricky at low power.

name: The Trapezium (Theta-1 Orionis)
colorDesc: Multiple Sapphire Blue Stars in M42
notes: The heart of the Great Orion Nebula! Four bright young stars (A, B, C, D) easily resolved at 50x in any small scope.

name: 23 Orionis
notes: Wide, pleasant pair in Orion's shoulder. Easily resolved at low powers.

name: Zeta Aquarii
notes: Binary star right on the celestial equator. Needing high power (100x-150x) and steady atmosphere.

name: 41 Aquarii
notes: Charming double star in Aquarius with 5.0" separation.

name: Iota Orionis
notes: Brightest star in Orion's Sword (south of M42). Wide companion easily split at 60x.

name: Sigma Orionis
notes: Part of a spectacular multiple star complex near Horsehead Nebula. Multiple components visible!

name: Xi Boötis
notes: Colorful nearby binary (22 light-years). Warm yellow primary with a cool reddish-orange secondary.

name: 61 Cygni (Bessel's Star)
notes: First star to have its parallax measured (Bessel in 1838). Very wide pair with rich fiery orange-red hues.

name: 52 Cygni
notes: Located right in front of the Western Veil Nebula (NGC 6960)! High contrast optical double.

name: 70 Ophiuchi
notes: Nearby binary star system (16.6 light-years). Warm yellow primary with a cool reddish-orange companion.

name: Alya
notes: Charming wide double star in the tail of the Serpent. Easily resolved at low powers.

name: Izar / Pulcherrima
notes: Otto Struve named it 'Pulcherrima' (Most Beautiful). Breathtaking orange primary with sapphire blue secondary.

name: Struve 747
notes: Located near Iota Orionis in Orion's Sword. Very wide pair, great target for small refractors.

name: Beta Monocerotis
notes: William Herschel's favorite triple star! Three blue-white gems forming an arc (A-B 7.3", B-C 2.8").

name: Kaffaljidhma
notes: Pretty tight pair requiring stable air and 100x+ power to split the companion out of yellow glare.

name: Struve 201
notes: Charming autumn double star in Cetus requiring 75mm+ aperture.

name: Iota Cassiopeiae
notes: Sensational triple star! Primary 4.6, B companion 6.9 at 2.6", C companion 8.4 at 7.2".

name: Struve 3053
notes: Very pretty gold and sapphire blue color contrast pair in circumpolar Cassiopeia.

name: Kappa Puppis
notes: Striking pair of bright twin blue-white supergiant stars easily resolved in low powers.

name: Rigil Kentaurus
notes: The nearest star system. Dazzling gold and orange pair, widening since the 2016 close approach toward a ~22″ maximum in the 2050s.

name: Acrux
notes: The flagship binary of the Southern Cross. Magnificent pair of brilliant B-type subgiants.

name: Epsilon Hydrae
notes: Rapid 15-year binary system. Requires good seeing and 100x+ to split the faint blue secondary.

name: Polaris (North Star)
notes: The Pole Star has a mag 8.7 companion 18.4" away. Never sets in northern skies. Easy test for 70mm scopes.

name: 36 Ophiuchi
notes: Twin orange K-dwarf stars (19.5 light-years away). Identical color and brightness.

name: Delta Serpentis
notes: Neat binary in the head of Serpens. Split nicely around 80x-100x.

name: Algorab
notes: High contrast color pair. Primary is a bright yellow-white subgiant with a faint purple companion.

name: Alula Australis
notes: Historic binary star system (60-year orbit). First binary system to have its orbit computed (by Herschel).

name: Delta Cephei
notes: Prototype Cepheid variable star! Accompanied by a wide blue companion at 41.0".

name: Rho Ophiuchi
notes: Illuminates the famous Rho Ophiuchi dust cloud. Pretty equal blue-white pair split nicely at 80x.

name: Iota Trianguli
notes: Yellow G-giant with a close yellow-white F-dwarf companion. Sometimes mislabeled Gamma Trianguli; the double is 6 Tri (ι Tri). Both components are themselves spectroscopic binaries.

name: Zeta Coronae Borealis
notes: Unusual subtle color hues! Soft celestial blue primary paired with pure white secondary.

name: Sigma Coronae Borealis
notes: Fine sun-like binary system in Corona Borealis separated by 7.0".

name: Mu Draconis (Arrakis)
notes: The real-life star 'Arrakis' (inspiration for Dune)! Twin white F-type stars split at 100x+.

name: Dziban
notes: Circumpolar northern pair with wide separation and gentle gold/violet color contrast.

name: 17 Draconis
notes: Neat double star in Draco split nicely at 90x.

name: 39 Draconis
notes: Charming double star in northern circumpolar Draco.

name: Bogardus (Theta Aurigae)
notes: Bright magnitude 2.6 star with a tight 7.2 companion. Glare test for 85mm-100mm refractors.

name: 14 Aurigae
notes: Pretty double star in Auriga easily resolved in small refractors.

name: Wasat
notes: Located near Pluto's discovery position (Clyde Tombaugh in 1930). White primary with orange dwarf secondary.

name: Kappa Geminorum
notes: Bright yellow giant primary with a dim companion requiring 75mm+ scope.

name: Tegmine
notes: Famous triple star! Pair A-B split at 5.9" (wide), while close companion A-B requires 100mm+ at 150x.

name: 24 Comae Berenices
notes: Underrated gems in Berenice's Hair! Gorgeous orange giant primary with sapphire blue secondary.

name: Nu Scorpii (Jabbah)
notes: The Southern Double-Double! Wide pair easily split at 40x; higher powers split both into sub-pairs!

name: Eta Lupi
notes: Southern showcase double star in Lupus. Sapphire blue primary with faint companion.

name: Xi Lupi
notes: Charming southern twin binary in Lupus.

name: Regor (Gamma Velorum)
notes: The brightest Wolf-Rayet star in the night sky! Dazzling blue primary with wide companion.

name: Struve 2816 (Garnet Cluster)
notes: Spectacular triple star embedded in the IC 1396 Elephant's Trunk Nebula region!

name: Chi Tauri
notes: Nice visual double star in northern Taurus near the Pleiades.

name: STF 655 (Lepus)
notes: Pretty double star in Lepus under Orion with a warm reddish-orange secondary.

name: Alnitak
notes: Easternmost Belt star, itself a tight pair of hot O stars. The bright primary makes this a good test of optics and seeing.

name: Meissa
notes: Orion's head: a crisp blue-white pair at the heart of a young star cluster, in a rich low-power field.

name: Eta Orionis
notes: Tight, nearly matched blue pair below Orion's Belt. Needs high power and steady air.

name: 38 Geminorum
notes: Pretty, unequal pair; use ~100x to pull the faint bluish companion away from the yellowish primary.

name: 32 Eridani
notes: A miniature Albireo of the winter sky: rich gold and blue at an easy separation. One of the finest color-contrast pairs.

name: 145 Canis Majoris
notes: The 'Winter Albireo': a wide, vivid orange-and-blue showpiece that splits in any telescope.

name: 38 Lyncis
notes: Bright white primary with a close companion tucked against it — a satisfying medium-power split.

name: 54 Leonis
notes: Easy, elegant white pair on the Lion's back; clean split at low power.

name: Kappa Boötis
notes: Wide and easy, with ι Boo in the same low-power field — a double treat.

name: Pi Boötis
notes: Neat, nearly matched white pair just south of Izar; among the loveliest sights in Boötes.

name: Antares
notes: Famous challenge: the 'green' companion hides in the red supergiant's glare. Try high power in steady air, or twilight.

name: Xi Scorpii
notes: A rewarding multiple: the bright star is itself a very close binary, and the wide pair Struve 1999 sits in the same field.

name: 95 Herculis
notes: The celebrated 'gold and silver' pair — two nearly equal stars with a subtle, beautiful color contrast.

name: Delta Cygni
notes: A classic test pair: the faint companion sits close to a brilliant primary. Wait for the steadiest moments.

name: Sheliak
notes: Wide, easy pair whose primary is a famous eclipsing binary, dipping from mag 3.3 to 4.4 every 13 days.

name: Zeta Lyrae
notes: Wide, easy pair in the same binocular field as Vega and the Double Double.

name: Psi1 Piscium
notes: Wide, well-matched white pair — an easy and satisfying split in any telescope.

name: 30 Arietis
notes: Wide pair of yellow-white F dwarfs; faint but easy, and the primary hosts a known exoplanet.

name: 94 Aquarii
notes: Pleasing yellow-orange pair of nearby sun-like stars, easily split at low power.

name: 8 Lacertae
notes: Anchor of a fine multiple system: the wide blue-white pair comes with fainter attendants for larger apertures.

name: Acamar
notes: One of the finest southern pairs: two brilliant white stars cleanly split in any telescope. Very low from mid-northern latitudes.

name: Mu Crucis
notes: Wide, easy blue pair in the Southern Cross — a binocular double from southern latitudes.

name: Kappa Lupi
notes: Wide, easy blue-white southern pair; splits at the lowest powers.

name: Pi Lupi
notes: Tight, perfectly matched blue pair — a fine high-power test from southern skies.

name: Zeta Herculis (Tianji)
notes: Famous fast binary (34.5-yr orbit) at the Keystone's corner, only 35 ly away. Now ~1.3" and closing: a 130mm+ challenge at 300x with a 2.7-mag brightness gap.

name: Epsilon Arietis
notes: A miniature Mesarthim: two nearly equal white A-type stars just 1.4" apart. A superb 100mm resolution test at 180x+.

name: Marfik
notes: Ophiuchus's elbow hides a tight 1.4" white binary (129-yr orbit). Needs 100mm+, high power, and steady air for a clean split.

name: Iota Leonis
notes: A 183-year binary that has been slowly widening for decades — now a fair test for 100mm scopes at high power, easier every year.

name: Pi Aquilae
notes: A neat, nearly equal 1.4" pair in the Eagle — a favorite summer 'mini-double' test for 100-130mm apertures.

name: 52 Orionis
notes: Perfectly matched 1.1" white twins east of Betelgeuse. A textbook Dawes-limit target for 100-125mm scopes at 200x+.

name: 33 Orionis
notes: Hot blue B-type pair at 1.9" north of Orion's Belt region. Splits cleanly in 90mm+ scopes on nights of good seeing.

name: Omega Leonis
notes: A demanding 118-year binary now near 0.9". Sub-arcsecond territory: 150mm+, 300x, and excellent seeing required — a true trophy split.

name: Tegmine AB (Close Pair)
notes: The famous 1.1" inner pair of the Tegmine triple (59.7-yr orbit). Splitting AB turns the easy wide double into a celebrated three-star showpiece.

name: Lambda Cygni
notes: One of the toughest bright pairs in Cygnus: 0.9" with a 1.6-mag gap. Reserved for 150mm+ apertures on nights of superb seeing.

name: Gamma Lupi
notes: A dazzling equal pair of hot B stars locked at just 0.8" (190-yr orbit). The southern sky's classic sub-arcsecond test — 150mm+ and rock-steady air.

name: 12 Lyncis
notes: A jewel-box triple: the tight 1.9" AB pair yields to 100mm at high power, while a 7.2-mag third star at 8.7" watches from nearby.

name: Mu-2 Boötis (Alkalurops BC)
notes: The faint 2.2" BC pair of the Alkalurops triple, with brilliant μ¹ shining 108" away. A lovely two-for-one at medium and high power.

name: Sigma Cassiopeiae
notes: A tight, unequal 3" pair of hot young stars at the western edge of Cassiopeia. Crisp split in 90mm+ at 150x on steady nights.

name: Sirius & The Pup
notes: The ultimate glare challenge: Sirius B, a mag 8.4 white dwarf, sits 11" from the sky's brightest star near maximum separation this decade. Use high power and place Sirius just outside the field.

name: Procyon & Its White Dwarf
notes: Legendary difficulty: mag 10.9 Procyon B hides just 5" from a star 15,000x brighter. Near its widest through the late 2020s — an occulting-bar or imaging quest for large apertures.

name: Keid (Omicron-2 Eridani)
notes: The easiest white dwarf in the sky! Mag 9.5 40 Eri B splits comfortably in small scopes, with a mag 11.2 red dwarf 9" from it — three stellar generations in one field.

name: Krueger 60
notes: One of the nearest binaries (13 ly): two dim red dwarfs in a 44.7-yr orbit, now slowly widening past 2". A 250mm+ trophy that visibly moves within a decade.

name: Struve 2398
notes: A genuine nearby red-dwarf binary only 11.5 ly away, split at 12". Faint but easy in 150mm — watch two embers of the solar neighborhood.

name: Groombridge 34
notes: A wide red-dwarf pair 11.6 ly away, both flare stars, both hosting known exoplanets. The mag 11.1 secondary needs 150mm+ and dark skies.

name: Regulus
notes: The Little King rules a wide court: its mag 8.1 orange companion (itself a close double) sits 3' away — easy in any telescope, striking despite the gulf in brightness.

name: S Monocerotis
notes: A blazing O-type star with a 3" companion, embedded in the Christmas Tree Cluster. Split the pair, then zoom out for one of winter's great star-fields.

name: Miram
notes: An underrated Albireo rival: a golden K supergiant with a mag 8.5 blue spark 28" away, set against a rich Milky Way field near the Double Cluster.

name: Enif
notes: The Horse's amber muzzle with a wide mag 8.7 companion. Swing the scope gently: the famous 'pendulum effect' makes the faint star seem to swing around Enif.

name: Struve 1999
notes: The quiet partner of the Xi Scorpii spectacle: this faint 12" orange pair shares the eyepiece with Xi, forming a rare double-double of unequal families.

name: Struve 1694
notes: A bright, wide white pair just 6.5° from Polaris — observable every night of the year. An easy, elegant split in any telescope, even 60mm.

name: 19 Lyncis
notes: A crisp, wide blue-white pair in the faint Lynx, with additional field stars forming a small chain. Rewarding at low power in any aperture.

name: 1 Camelopardalis
notes: Two massive young B stars split at 10" in the dim Giraffe — an easy target that anchors a pretty low-power field near the open cluster NGC 1502.

name: p Eridani
notes: A beautiful matched pair of orange K dwarfs only 26 ly away, gliding through a 475-yr orbit. A far-southern gem, easy in any scope from low latitudes.

name: Theta Indi
notes: The finest double in the far-southern Indus: a clean 7" split with a pleasing 2.7-mag contrast, well placed on spring evenings south of the equator.

name: Upsilon Carinae
notes: A bright, easy 5" southern pair inside the Diamond Cross asterism, surrounded by the Carina Milky Way — a showcase field at any magnification.
